common_name: Silk Hope Mulberry (Southern Heirloom Black Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade; Silk Hope is a Southern heirloom black mulberry passed down through generations of home orchards for its rich, wine-dark fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Silk Hope is a Southern heirloom black mulberry, named for the small North Carolina community where it was long cultivated and passed down among home orchardists for its rich, deep-purple-black fruit and dependable production. The elongated berries are intensely sweet with a wine-like depth of flavor considered by many mulberry enthusiasts to surpass the milder white and red mulberry types more commonly sold. Like other black mulberries it is somewhat slower-growing and less cold-hardy than white mulberry hybrids, but well suited to Gulf South heat and long growing seasons once established. Trees tolerate poor soil and drought once established, needing little more than occasional deep watering during extended dry spells. Site female-fruiting trees well away from patios, walkways, and parked cars, since the ripe, juicy berries drop over an extended summer harvest window and stain hard surfaces.
sources: Southern heirloom fruit tree nursery variety records

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Kokuso is a Japanese mulberry selection bred for unusually large, richly flavored fruit rather than the leaf production most Morus alba selections were historically bred for.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Kokuso is a Japanese mulberry cultivar bred specifically for dessert-quality fruit rather than the silkworm-feeding leaf production most Morus alba selections were traditionally grown for. The berries are notably large, dark purple-black, and richly sweet with good depth of flavor, ripening over a fairly extended summer window that spreads out the harvest rather than concentrating it into a short flush. Trees are vigorous and adaptable to a wide range of soils, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil once established with only occasional deep watering needed during extended dry spells. Because mulberries can grow quite large and dense if left unpruned, an annual shaping prune in late winter keeps the canopy at a manageable height for easier harvest. Site female-fruiting trees away from patios, walkways, and parked cars, since ripe berries drop over an extended period and stain hard surfaces.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Mulberry Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade; Tehama is a California heirloom black mulberry known for exceptionally large, richly flavored fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Tehama is a California heirloom black mulberry named for Tehama County, prized among fruit collectors for producing some of the largest berries of any black mulberry selection, often two inches or more in length, with an intensely rich, wine-dark, sweet-tart flavor typical of Morus nigra at its best. Like other black mulberries it grows more slowly and stays somewhat more compact than the vigorous white mulberry hybrids, making it a reasonable choice where space is limited, though it still eventually forms a substantial shade tree. Trees tolerate heat, drought, and average soil once established, needing only occasional deep watering during extended dry spells. Site female-fruiting trees well away from patios, walkways, and parked cars, since the ripe, juicy berries drop over an extended summer harvest window and stain hard surfaces.

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes fall through early spring in moist, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun; Wilder is an older American red currant cultivar valued for productivity and long, well-filled fruit clusters.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade helpful in warmer climates; Wilder is an older American red currant cultivar long grown for its productivity and long, evenly filled clusters (strigs) of bright red, tart-sweet berries. It is self-fertile and bears reliably without a second bush for pollination, making it a practical single-plant choice for a small garden. Fruit is excellent for jelly, syrup, and baking, with the classic bright, tart currant flavor that mellows only somewhat with full ripeness. Because red currants fruit mainly on spurs of two- and three-year-old wood rather than new growth, prune to an open, vase-shaped framework each winter and remove any wood older than three years to keep the bush vigorous and productive. Net the bushes as fruit ripens, since birds are strongly drawn to currants.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Currant and Gooseberry Production
